artboards.title: The list — shared by D, E and F
Option D — the team gets its own page
Option E — a panel over the list
Option F — the row unfolds in place

annotations.text:
THE BRIEF, from your last note

· keep the page header — eyebrow, title, the description
· a big Create a team button at the top
· teams listed one by one in a table, like recordings
· clicking one opens its members: add, remove, roles, and the rest of the team's options

This artboard is the LIST, and it is the same in all three options — it is the detail step that differs. The table is the Recordings table's own anatomy: same grid, same row border, same 10.5px column labels.

WHY B DIDN'T SURVIVE CONTACT

On your real data it was two cards in a three-column grid, so most of the page was empty — and the activity bars, which were the whole argument for cards, collapsed into stubs because one person had 23 runs and the other had none.

Cards flatter a full team and expose a small one. A table does the opposite, which is the right way round: you start small.

OPTION D — the team gets its own page

/team/:id, reached from Open. Full width for the members table, room for shared skills and a proper settings block, and Delete sits in that block rather than loose at the bottom of the page.

Best for: teams you actually administer — everything about one team in one place, and it has an address you can link or bookmark.
Tradeoff: a real navigation. Comparing two teams means going back and forth.

OPTION E — a panel over the list

The list stays behind, so moving between teams is one click each and you never lose your place.

Best for: several teams and quick edits — add somebody here, fix a role there.
Tradeoff: 560px is narrow, so per-person activity shrinks to one line of text, and it is the least comfortable of the three for a team of twenty.

OPTION F — the row unfolds in place

No navigation and no overlay: the row opens and the team appears underneath it, the same gesture the Recordings table already uses for its replay knobs.

Best for: one page that does everything, and a product that already taught this gesture on another screen.
Tradeoff: the page gets long with several teams open, and there is nowhere obvious to put anything that needs real room later.

In all three: the invitation is a row in the members list, not a separate section — a person who is not here yet. Roles stay editable in place for an owner. Rename and Delete are together, away from everyday actions. And every option keeps the sentence about what a team does not open, because that is the part people are actually uneasy about.

Mixing is fine: F's gesture with D's page for teams past a certain size is a real answer.
